title: Personal financial statements, budgeting and emergency funds
objectives: Prepare a net worth and cash-flow statement.
Apply the savings, debt-service and liquidity ratios.
body_md:
## Two statements

**Balance sheet (net worth):** assets (cash, investments, property) minus liabilities (loans, cards).

**Cash-flow statement:** income minus expenses and EMIs gives the **surplus** available to invest.

## Key ratios

| Ratio | Formula | Rule of thumb |
|---|---|---|
| **Savings rate** | Savings ÷ income | 20% or more |
| **Debt-service ratio** | EMIs ÷ income | Below about 40% |
| **Liquidity ratio** | Liquid assets ÷ monthly expenses | At least 6 months |
| **Solvency ratio** | Net worth ÷ total assets | Higher is safer |

## Emergency fund

Hold **3 to 6 months of expenses** (more for variable income) in liquid, safe options before taking risk. Insurance and an emergency fund come **before** equity SIPs.

## Steps

1. Gather income, expenses, assets and liabilities from documents.
2. Separate **needs, wants and goals**.
3. Compute the ratios, flag problems (high EMIs, no cover).
4. Set the surplus aside for goals by priority.

## Why it matters

Advice built on a wrong or incomplete picture is unsuitable even if the products are good.

> **Exam tip:** Emergency fund first; EMIs above about 40% of income signal stress.
example: Income ₹1 lakh a month, EMIs ₹45,000: the debt-service ratio is 45%, above the 40% comfort level, so reduce debt before adding new investments.
say: Before investing, let us build a six-month cash buffer.
Your EMIs take almost half your income, so we should address that first.
never: Put the whole emergency fund into equity for growth.
Ratios do not matter if returns are high.

check.q: A common emergency fund target is:
check.why: Three to six months of expenses.
